explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose
   - Jekyll is a static‐site generator implemented as a Ruby gem and CLI tool.  
   - Purpose: transform a directory of source files (Markdown, Liquid templates, data files, assets) into a static website.

2. High-level architecture components
   a. CLI layer
      • exe/jekyll – command‐line entry point; dispatches subcommands (build, serve, new, etc.)  
      • lib/jekyll/commands – each command implements building, serving, cleaning, etc.  
   b. Configuration loader
      • lib/jekyll/configuration.rb – merges defaults, _config.yml, front matter, CLI flags  
   c. File readers
      • lib/jekyll/readers/* – discover and read pages, posts, collections, data files, static files, theme assets  
   d. Converter pipeline
      • lib/jekyll/converters/* – chain of converters (Markdown via Kramdown, Sass, Smartypants, etc.)  
   e. Liquid rendering
      • lib/jekyll/liquid_renderer – render templates and pages using Liquid; exposes “drops” (context objects)  
   f. Generator & publisher
      • lib/jekyll/generator – orchestrates conversion, rendering, and writes output to _site  
      • lib/jekyll/publisher – writes files, handles asset copying, applies permalinks  
   g. Plugin system
      • lib/jekyll/plugin_manager & plugin hooks – load third-party extensions, custom converters, generators, tags, filters  
   h. Development server
      • lib/jekyll/commands/serve – built-in WEBrick server, live-reload reactor, websockets  
   i. Themes & templates
      • lib/blank_template, lib/site_template, lib/theme_template – bundled scaffolding for new sites and themes  
   j. External dependencies & tools
      • Ruby interpreter, Liquid template engine, Kramdown, Rouge, WEBrick, external gems as defined in jekyll.gemspec  

3. Relationships and data flow
   1. User invokes `jekyll build` or `jekyll serve` via CLI  
   2. CLI loads Configuration loader → merges configs  
   3. Plugin Manager loads plugins/hooks  
   4. File Readers scan the source directory for pages, posts, data, assets, theme files  
   5. Converter Pipeline transforms raw content (Markdown→HTML, Sass→CSS, etc.)  
   6. Liquid Renderer applies layouts, includes, drops/context  
   7. Generator orchestrates and calls Publisher  
   8. Publisher writes static output into the _site directory  
   9. (If serving) Development server serves _site, monitors changes, triggers rebuilds  

   Use directional arrows to show this stepwise flow.

4. Architectural patterns & principles
   - Pipeline/chain of responsibility for converters  
   - Plugin-oriented architecture: hook points at reading, conversion, rendering, site generation  
   - Modular layering: configuration → I/O (readers) → processing (converters, renderer) → output (publisher)  
   - Separation of concerns: command dispatch, config, I/O, transformation, rendering, serving  

5. Tailoring the diagram to a CLI/static‐site‐generator
   - Emphasize the build pipeline: config → readers → converters → renderer → publisher  
   - Highlight plugin extension points alongside each stage  
   - Show optional serve component branching off publisher to WEBrick + live‐reload  
   - Include theme/template as an input alongside site source  

6. Diagram notation guidelines
   - Components as labeled boxes (e.g., “Configuration Loader,” “File Reader,” “Converter Pipeline,” “Liquid Renderer,” “Publisher,” “Plugin Manager,” “WEBrick Server”)  
   - Use directional arrows to indicate data flow and dependencies  
   - Color‐code layers (e.g., green for core engine, blue for plugin/extensions, orange for I/O, purple for rendering)  
   - Optionally use different shapes for static assets (cylinder for data, document icons for content)  

7. Detail and completeness
   - Annotate each arrow with the type of data passed (e.g., “raw markdown files,” “HTML fragments,” “rendered pages”)  
   - List key technologies/frameworks near each component (e.g., Kramdown under Converter, Liquid under Renderer)  
   - Capture all subcomponents: commands (build, serve, new), readers (page, post, data), converters (markdown, Sass), plugin hooks  

By following these guidelines, your system design diagram will accurately represent Jekyll’s architecture—its layered build pipeline, extensibility via plugins, and built-in development server—while clearly showing how source content is transformed into a static website.  
</explanation>
